(p-135)Surah al-Buruj (The Constellations)

Makkan, and its verses are twenty-two.

﴿By the sky containing the constellations﴾. The constellations (al-buruj) are the twelve signs, which are likened to palaces, because the planets descend into them and the fixed stars are in them, or the stations of the moon (manazil al-qamar), or the great stars. They were called buruj (sing. burj, "tower" or "mansion") because of their prominence (zuhur), or they are the gates of the sky, for the descending (nawazil) emanations come out from them. The root meaning of the word is prominence and manifestness.
﴿And by the promised Day﴾, i.e., the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And by a witness and that which is witnessed﴾: that is, whoever bears witness on that Day among the creatures, and the marvels that are present therein. Their being indefinite (nakrah) serves to indicate vagueness in description, meaning: a witness and a witnessed thing whose description cannot be fully comprehended; or it serves to express exaggeration in multiplicity. It has been said: the witness is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the witnessed is the Day of Resurrection. It has been said: it is Jesus (peace be upon him) and his community, based on the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And I was a witness over them﴾ ... etc. It has been said: the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) and all the other nations. It has been said: the Day of Tarwiyah and the Day of 'Arafah. It has been said: the Day of 'Arafah and the Day of Friday. It has been said: the Black Stone and the pilgrims. It has been said: the days and nights and the children of Adam. And from al-Hasan: "There is no day but that it calls out: 'I am a new day, and I am a witness over what is done in me, so seize me, for if my sun sets, it will not overtake me until the Day of Resurrection.'" It has been said: the guardian angels and the children of Adam. It has been said: the prophets and Muhammad (peace be upon them all).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 85, verse 4:

﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench.﴾ It has been said: this is the answer to the oath, with the lam omitted from it because of its length. The original is "la-qutila" (لَقُتِلَ), as in the words of one who said:

؎ I swore to her by God an oath of a sinner ∗∗∗ "They slept, and there was no talk nor any sound."

It has also been said: its implied form is "laqad qutila" (لَقَدْ قُتِلَ). In any case, the sentence is informative (khabariyya), but the more apparent view is that it is supplicatory (du'a'iyya), indicating the answer. It is as if it were said: "I swear by these things that they, that is, the disbelievers of Makkah, are cursed, just as the companions of the trench were cursed." This is because the surah was revealed to strengthen the believers in the faith they held, and in their patience upon it, and to make them patient in the face of the harm of the disbelievers. It also reminds them of what befell those before them of torment for faith, and of their patience in that, so that they may take them as an example, be patient over what they encountered from their people, and know that these people, in the sight of God, Mighty and Majestic, are of the same standing as those tormented, cursed like them, deserving that what was said about those be said about them. It is also read "quttila" (قُتِّلَ) with shadda. "Al-ukhdud" (الأُخْدُودُ) is a ditch dug in the ground, a cleft and the like, in the form "fu'ul" (بِناءً), and its meaning corresponds to "al-khaqq" (الخَقِّ) and "al-ukhquq" (الأُخْقُوقِ).

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that one of the kings had a sorcerer. When he grew old, he sent a boy to him to teach him sorcery. On the boy's way was a monk, and he listened to him. One day, on his way, he saw an animal that had blocked the people. It was said: the animal was a lion. So he took a stone and said: "O God, if the monk is more beloved to You than the sorcerer, then kill it." So he killed it. After that, the boy would heal the blind-born and the leper, and cure other ailments. A companion of the king went blind, and he healed him. The king saw him and asked: "Who restored your sight?" He said: "My Lord." So the king became angry and tortured him, and he pointed to the boy. The boy was tortured and pointed to the monk. The monk did not turn back from his religion, so he was sawn in two with a saw. The boy refused, so he was taken to a mountain to be thrown from its peak. He supplicated, and the mountain shook with the people, and they fell, and he was saved. He was taken to a boat (qurqur, قُرْقُورٍ) and they sailed out with him in order to drown him. He supplicated, and the boat capsized with them, and they drowned, and he was saved. He said to the king: "You will not kill me until you gather the people in an open ground, crucify me on a trunk, take an arrow from my quiver, and say: 'In the name of God, Lord of the boy,' then shoot me with it." So he shot him, and it struck his temple. He placed his hand upon it and died. The people said: "We believe in the Lord of the boy." It was said to the king: "What you were wary of has befallen you." So he commanded trenches (akhadid, أخاديد) to be dug at the mouths of the alleys, and fires were kindled in them. Whoever did not return, he threw into them. Then came a woman with a child, and she hesitated. The child said: "O mother, be patient, for you are upon the truth," so she plunged in. It was also said: he said to her: "Stay, and do not be hypocritical; it is but a moment," so she was patient.

It was said: the boy was taken out of his grave in the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, and his finger was upon his temple just as he had placed it when he was killed.

And from Ali, may God be pleased with him: that one of the kings of the Magians had intercourse with his sister while he was drunk. When he sobered up, he regretted it and sought a way out. His sister said to him: "The way out is that you address the people and say: 'God has permitted the marriage of sisters,' and then after that address them, saying: 'God has forbidden it.'" So he addressed them, but they did not accept from him. She said to him: "Unleash the whip upon them." He did so, but they did not accept. She said: "Unleash the sword upon them." He did so, but they did not accept. So he commanded the trenches and the kindling of fire, and threw into them whoever refused. These are the ones whom God, may He be exalted, meant by His saying: ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench.﴾

It was also said: a man who was of the religion of Jesus, peace be upon him, came to Najran, and he called the people, and they responded to him. Then Dhu Nuwas the Jew marched against them with troops from Himyar. He gave them the choice between the fire and Judaism, but they refused. So he burned twelve thousand of them in the trenches. It was also said: seventy thousand. And it is mentioned that the length of the trench was forty cubits, and its width twelve cubits.

﴿the fire﴾ is a *badal ishtimal* (a substitute of inclusion, in which the substituted noun contains what it replaces) for *al-Ukhdud*.

﴿full of fuel﴾ is a description of it, indicating its extreme greatness, the height of its flames, and the abundance of what it requires of firewood and of people's bodies. It was also recited as الوَقُودُ with a *ḍamma* (*al-wuqūd*).

The phrase ﴿إذْ هم عَلَيْها قُعُودٌ﴾ is a temporal adverb (ẓarf) modifying "قُتِلَ", meaning: they were cursed at the time when they surrounded the fire, sitting around it in a place overlooking it, from the edges of the trench (al-Ukhdud), as in the verse:

Wa bāta ʿalā al-nāri al-nadā wa al-muḥalliqu
"And al-Nadā and al-Muḥalliq spent the night over the fire."

(p-137) ﴿And they, over what they do to the believers, are witnesses﴾. That is: some of them testify for others before the King that none of them fell short in what he was commanded to do. Or it means that they are witnesses who will testify to what they did to the believers on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿on the Day when their tongues and their hands will testify against them﴾. It has also been said that ʿalā (on, over) here carries the meaning of maʿa (with), so the meaning is: they, along with what they do to the believers of punishment, are present, showing no mercy toward them because of the extreme hardness of their hearts. This is what the noble text (al-naẓm al-karīm) calls for, and what the well-known reports (al-riwāyāt al-mashhūra) confirm. It has been reported that when the tyrants (al-jabābira) threw the believers into the fire while they sat around it, the fire caught hold of them and burned them, while Allah, Mighty and Majestic, saved the believers from it unharmed. This view was held by al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and al-Wāḥidī, and on this basis they interpreted His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾.

**[Verse 8]** *"And they did not resent them for anything"*: that is, they did not object to them or find fault with them.

*"Except that they believed in Allah, the Almighty, the Praiseworthy"*: this is a resumptive clause (*istiʾnaf*, a new sentence that resumes the thought without grammatical dependence on what precedes it), which makes clear their complete innocence of anything that is faulted or objected to. It follows the pattern of the poet's words:

*"There is no fault in them, except that their guests*
*are blamed for forgetting beloved ones and homeland."*

Describing Him, exalted is He, as *ʿAziz* (Almighty), meaning Mighty and Overpowering, whose punishment is to be feared, and as *Hamid* (Praiseworthy), meaning Bountiful, whose reward is to be hoped for, and confirming this with His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 85, verse 9:

﴿Him to Whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth.﴾ This is to indicate the basis (manat) of their faith. And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And Allah is, over all things, Witness.﴾ is a promise for them and a severe warning for those who torment them, for His knowledge, exalted is He, of all things, among which are the deeds of both groups, necessarily entails the full recompense of each of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 85, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women﴾ i.e., they afflicted them in their religion in order to make them turn back from it. The intended referents are either the People of the Trench specifically, with "those who were persecuted" meaning those thrown into the trench, or it refers to those who tested them with harm and torture in general, and they are included in the group by primary inclusion (dukhul awwaliyy).

﴿Then they did not repent﴾ i.e., from their disbelief and their persecution. For the persecution in religion mentioned cannot be conceived of except from a disbeliever, with certainty. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿for them is the punishment of Hell﴾ is a clause that serves as the predicate of "inna" (indeed), or the predicate is "for them," and "punishment" is raised by it as the agent (fa'iliyya), which is the better reading. The fa' (then) is because the subject contains the meaning of a conditional (shart), and there is no harm in its being abrogated by "inna" (naskh bi-inna), although al-Akhfash disagreed. The meaning: for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of Hell because of their disbelief.

﴿And for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾ and it is another great fire, because of their persecution of the believers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 85, verse 11:

﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ (is) on an absolute basis, (applying to) those who were tested and others. "For them" (is) because of what has been mentioned of faith and righteous deeds.

﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. If by "gardens" is meant the trees, then the flowing of rivers beneath them is evident. If by them is meant the ground upon which they stand, then the description (lit. "greeting," al-tahiyya) is by way of its apparent part, for its trees cover its open area, as the name "Jannah" (Garden) indicates; its explanation has been given many times before. "That" (dhalika) is a demonstrative, either referring to the described gardens, and the masculine form (taknir) is due to its interpretation as "what has been mentioned"; this is to indicate that the basis of the ruling is their title, which is what competitors compete for. For the demonstrative pronoun points to the essence of the one indicated in terms of his being characterized by the attributes mentioned, not merely to his essence as the pronoun does. So when the gardens are indicated in terms of their having been mentioned, their stated title has necessarily been taken into account. Or it refers to what is implied by the words of the Exalted: ﴿For them are gardens﴾ ...etc., namely their possession of them, for their attaining them necessarily entails their possessing them, certainly, and whichever it is. Thus the meaning of distance in it is to signal the loftiness of its rank and the remoteness of its station in excellence and nobility. Its position is nominative, as the subject of the inchoative, and its predicate is what follows it, i.e., "that," the mentioned, greatly important matter.

﴿The great triumph﴾, in which the world and everything in it of kinds of desires, in its entirety, becomes insignificant. And "fawz" means salvation from evil and attainment of good. On the first meaning it is a verbal noun used for the object for emphasis; on the second meaning it remains a verbal noun in its own form.

Translation:

﴿Indeed, the seizing of your Lord is severe.﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, to signify that the disbelievers of his people have a considerable share of its import, as is indicated by the mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyyah) together with its attribution to his pronoun, peace and blessings be upon him. Al-batsh (the seizing) is taking hold with force. Since it is described as severe (shadid), it has been multiplied and intensified: it is His seizing of the tyrants and wrongdoers, and His taking them with punishment and retribution, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they are wrongdoers. Indeed, His seizing is painful and severe.﴾

Indeed, it is He who originates and repeats (creation).

Meaning: He originates the creation and He repeats it, with no one having any share in either of them. In this there is further confirmation of the severity of His seizing (of the wrongdoers). Or, it means: He initiates the seizing (punishment) of the disbelievers in this world and repeats it in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 85, verse 14:

﴿And He is the All-Forgiving﴾ to whoever repents and believes.

﴿the Most Loving﴾, the one who loves whoever obeys Him.

Dhu al-'Arsh (the Lord of the Throne): its Creator. It was also said: by "the Throne" is meant "the King," i.e., the Possessor of overpowering dominion. It is recited as "Dhi al-'Arsh" (in the genitive), being an attribute of "Rabbika" (your Lord).

Al-Majid (the Glorious): the Mighty in His essence and His attributes, for He is necessarily existent (wajib al-wujud), perfect in power, and complete in wisdom. It is also recited in the genitive (al-Majidi), as an attribute of "Rabbika" or of "al-'Arsh," and its majd (glory) is His exaltedness and His greatness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 85, verse 16:

﴿Doer of whatever He wills﴾, in such a way that nothing among His actions, may He be exalted, or the actions of others, is ever left behind by His will; and it is the predicate (khabar) of a deleted subject (mubtada').

(p-139) His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Has the story of the hosts reached you?﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*) that establishes the severity of God's seizing (*batsh*) of the wrongdoing, disobedient, disbelieving, and tyrannical. His being "one who does whatever He wills" (*fa'ʿāl li-mā yurīd*) includes a consolation for him, peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ), by indicating that He will afflict his people with what befell the hosts.

"Pharaoh and Thamud." [This is] an apposition (badal) to "the hosts," because by Pharaoh is meant him and his people, and by their story is meant what proceeded from them of persistence in disbelief and error, and what befell them of punishment and retribution. The meaning is: their story has come to you, and you have known what they did and what was done to them. So remind your people of the affairs of God Most High, and warn them that there may befall them the like of what befell their counterparts.

The words of His, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve are in denial﴾. This is a turning away (idrab) from the comparison of them to those mentioned before, and a clarification that they are worse than them in disbelief and transgression. As if it were said: they are not like them in that; rather, they are more deserving of punishment and more liable to retribution than them, for they are persistently in severe denial of the Noble Qur'an. Or it was said: their offence is not merely the lack of remembrance and admonition by what they heard of their accounts, but rather they are, along with that, in severe denial of the Qur'an which speaks of that. Yet this is not because they deny the occurrence of the event, but because of its being a Qur'an from Allah, exalted is He, despite the clarity of its matter and the manifestness of its condition through its dazzling proofs.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And Allah encompasses them from behind them﴾ ... Let me translate the passage.

﴿And Allah, from behind them, is all-encompassing﴾ is an illustration (tamthil) of their not being saved from the might of Allah, the Exalted, by the impossibility of the encompassed escaping the Encompasser.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 85, verse 21:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an﴾ is a rejection of their disbelief, a refutation of their denial, and an affirmation of the truth. That is: the matter is not as they said; rather, it is a noble book of lofty rank among the divine books in both its composition (nazm) and its meaning. It has also been read as "Qur'anu majidin" with the genitive construction, meaning: the Qur'an of a glorious Lord.

ﷻ﴿فِي لَوْحٍ مَحْفُوظٍ﴾ [In a Preserved Tablet] — that is, protected from distortion and from the reach of the devils. It is also read as "مَحْفُوظٌ" (maḥfūẓun) with a nominative ending, as an attribute of "قُرْآنٍ" (Qur'an), and it is read as "فِي لَوْحٍ" (fī lawḥin), where "لَوْحٌ" (lawḥ, tablet) means the air, that is, what is above the seventh heaven, in which the Tablet is located.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Buruj, Allah the Exalted will give him, for the number of every Friday and of the Day of 'Arafah that occurs in this world, ten good deeds."
